newsitem.title: USA: Timet's new cash pile to boost output.
newsitem.headline: Timet's new cash pile to boost output.

text.p: Cash from Titanium Metals Corp's sale of convertible preferred stock, whose pricing was announced Thursday, will cut corporate debt and fund a production hike to tackle lengthening order backlogs, the company said.
"The paper was very much in demand," said Joe Compofelice, Timet's chief financial officer.

The placement raised $175 million, with $100 million going to pay company debt, and $25 million to raise output. An over allotment option granted to the underwriters could raise the total to $201 million within a few days.

"People see titanium requirements for aerospace being quite strong, and people focused on the entire titanium business see the opportunity for non-aerospace business to overtake aerospace business by the year 2000."
"The backlog of aircraft orders on Boeing, Airbus and McDonnell Douglas' books was about 2,400, including the latest US Air order, Compofelice estimated.
"We would not expect commercial airline deliveries to peak until some time after the year 2000," Compofelice said. "In the case of Timet, it's by far the highest backlog of orders we have ever had."
This year Timet will produce some 29 million pounds or 13,154 tonnes of titanium products. Analysts expected this to reach 34 million pounds or 15,422 tonnes in 1997.
Oregon Metallurgical told a recent industry conference that global titanium sponge and scrap supply this year would reach 285 million pounds, rising to 355 million in the year 2000.
Sponge and scrap demand would rise from 260 million to 333 million over the same period.
Oregon said world titanium products market should rise from 110 million pounds this year to 150 million in 2000.

The boom in titanium prompted Timet to restart its Kroll process sponge plant earlier this year. The Kroll plant's output should reach 10 million pounds on an annual rate by mid-1997, pushing Timet's sponge production capacity from the current level of 22 million pounds up to 32 million pounds.
Compofelice expected next year's output of sponge - an intermediate product which is melted into ingot or slab to roll into bar, strip or sheet - to reach 25 million pounds.
Most of Timet's output is from its cheaper and newer vacuum distillation process which operates at 20 million pounds a year of its rated 22 million pounds capacity.
The company also bought some 15 million pounds of sponge on the open market this year to plug that gap between its own production and total mill product output.

"We have intentionally struck a balance of working towards making about 60 percent of our sponge, and buying about 40 percent so that we can continually have the lowest cost structure," Compofelice said.
"We will be producing more and buying more next year," he added.
Timet will also raise capacity at its electron beam melting plant from 33 million pounds a year to 53 million pounds from the second half of 1998 to avoid a bottleneck due to higher sponge capacity.

The melting plant processes the sponge into slab and ingot. The electron beam plant was recently acquired from Johnson Matthey and will help Timet cut costs because it can be fed sponge or scrap titanium, Compofelice said.
